title: Ego Is the Enemy
author: Ryan Holiday
blurb: Ryan Holiday argues that ego, an unhealthy belief in our own importance, quietly sabotages us whether we are starting out, succeeding or failing. Drawing on Stoic philosophy and stories from history, sport and business, he splits the book into three parts. In Aspire, he warns against talking instead of working, chasing status over purpose, and thinking we already know enough. In Success, he shows how pride, entitlement and a flattering story about ourselves make us lose focus on what really matters. In Failure, he explains how ego turns setbacks into self-pity, and how humility lets us learn and recover. The answer is not self-hatred but sobriety: honest self-assessment, steady work, and judging ourselves by our own standards rather than applause. The goal is to keep ego small so the work can be big.

lessons.b: Ego, an unhealthy belief in our own importance, undermines us at every stage, whether we are aspiring, succeeding or failing.
Talking about our plans gives us the feeling of progress without the effort, draining the energy we need to actually do the work.
Through the story of military strategist John Boyd, Holiday asks whether we want to be someone important or to do something that matters, because the two often conflict.

Like fighter Frank Shamrock's rule of having someone better to learn from, someone equal to test yourself against, and someone less skilled to teach, lasting growth requires believing you still have much to learn.
Early on, helping others succeed and clearing paths for them builds skill and relationships far faster than demanding credit.

lessons.b: Jackie Robinson's choice not to retaliate against abuse shows that controlling our pride and reactions can be a source of real strength.
Once we succeed, telling ourselves a neat story of destiny makes us arrogant, so we should keep focusing on the daily standards that created success, as coach Bill Walsh did.
Without clarity about what truly matters to us, ego pushes us to chase more money, status and wins, leaving us restless and unfulfilled.
When failure or hardship strikes, we can waste the time waiting or use it to learn and grow, as Malcolm X did by reading and studying in prison.
Ego is a recurring cycle, and the lasting cure is to judge ourselves by our own standards of effort and integrity rather than outside praise or results.
